disease.name: Vitamin B12 Deficiency (Cobalamin Deficiency)
disease.scientific_name: Vitamin B12 Deficiency / Cobalamin Deficiency / Hypocobalaminaemia / Megaloblastic Anaemia / Pernicious Anaemia / Subacute Combined Degeneration of Spinal Cord
disease.icd_10_code: E53.8 (Deficiency of other specified B vitamins — Vitamin B12 deficiency); D51.0 (Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia due to intrinsic factor deficiency — Pernicious anaemia); D51.1 (Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia due to selective malabsorption); D51.3 (Other dietary vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia); D51.9 (Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia, unspecified); G32.0 (Subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord in diseases classified elsewhere); G62.0 (Drug-induced polyneuropathy — metformin/nitrous oxide B12 deficiency neuropathy); G31.8 (Nutritional B12 deficiency dementia)
disease.category: Haematology / Neurology / Nutritional Medicine / Endocrinology / Public Health

overview.description: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency is a widespread nutritional and metabolic disorder arising from inadequate intake, impaired absorption, or defective cellular utilisation of Vitamin B12 — an essential water-soluble micronutrient required for three fundamental biological processes: (1) DNA synthesis and cell division — deficiency causes megaloblastic changes in all rapidly dividing cells, most dramatically manifested as megaloblastic anaemia; (2) myelin synthesis and neurological integrity — deficiency causes progressive demyelination of the spinal cord (subacute combined degeneration — SACD) and peripheral nerves, producing potentially irreversible neurological disability; (3) one-carbon metabolism — as methylcobalamin, B12 is the cofactor for methionine synthase (converting homocysteine to methionine) and as adenosylcobalamin for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase — both essential for cell metabolism. Vitamin B12 is produced exclusively by microorganisms and is present naturally only in animal-derived foods (meat, fish, poultry, eggs, dairy). Plants do not contain B12 (with negligible exceptions such as fermented and certain seaweed products). This single biological fact — that B12 is absent from plant foods — makes India, the world's largest vegetarian nation, the most severely affected country globally for B12 deficiency. It is estimated that 47-81% of Indian adults and children have inadequate B12 status, with frank deficiency (serum B12 <200 pg/mL) in approximately 30-50% of urban and rural populations — a public health catastrophe of enormous proportions that remains dramatically underappreciated and underdiagnosed. Beyond dietary factors, two key medical causes drive B12 deficiency in India: pernicious anaemia (autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells — eliminating intrinsic factor production and with it, B12 absorption) and METFORMIN therapy (the most widely prescribed antidiabetic drug in India — which reduces B12 absorption in up to 30% of long-term users through a mechanism impairing the calcium-dependent absorption of the IF-B12 complex at the terminal ileum). The clinical spectrum of B12 deficiency ranges from asymptomatic biochemical deficiency (detected only by blood testing) to megaloblastic anaemia (fatigue, pallor, breathlessness) to devastating neurological consequences (peripheral neuropathy; subacute combined degeneration — SACD — with progressive spastic weakness and loss of coordination; dementia; and psychiatric disturbance) that may become irreversible if diagnosis is delayed beyond months. The fundamental tragedy of B12 deficiency in India is its PREVENTABILITY — daily supplementation with cyanocobalamin or methylcobalamin costs less than Rs 2-5 per day, making this one of the most cost-effective nutritional interventions available.
overview.affected_organ: Red blood cells (haematopoietic system — bone marrow); spinal cord (dorsal and lateral columns); peripheral nerves; brain (cognitive function); gastric mucosa; oral mucosa (tongue); cardiovascular system (via homocysteine elevation); reproductive system (infertility); fetal neural tube (maternal deficiency)

b12_biochemistry.forms: Cyanocobalamin (synthetic — stable; used in supplements and fortification); Hydroxocobalamin (natural; used in IM injections — longer tissue retention); Methylcobalamin and Adenosylcobalamin (the TWO ACTIVE coenzyme forms in human cells)
b12_biochemistry.methylcobalamin_function: Cofactor for METHIONINE SYNTHASE — converts homocysteine to methionine (regenerating tetrahydrofolate — the active folate form for DNA synthesis); deficiency causes: elevated homocysteine (cardiovascular risk); functional folate deficiency (explains why B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia despite normal folate); impaired myelin synthesis (methionine → SAM → methylation reactions in myelin)
b12_biochemistry.adenosylcobalamin_function: Cofactor for METHYLMALONYL-CoA MUTASE — converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in fatty acid and amino acid catabolism; deficiency causes: methylmalonic acid (MMA) accumulation — the most specific biochemical marker of B12 deficiency; impaired myelin production
b12_biochemistry.daily_requirement: Adults: 2.4 mcg/day (ICMR recommendation); Pregnant women: 2.6 mcg/day; Lactating women: 2.8 mcg/day; Infants 0-6 months: 0.4 mcg/day; Children 1-3 years: 0.9 mcg/day; 4-8 years: 1.2 mcg; 9-13 years: 1.8 mcg
b12_biochemistry.body_stores: Total body B12 store: 2-5 mg (predominantly in liver — 60-80%); daily requirement is only 2-4 mcg; stores can sustain the body for 2-5 YEARS after complete B12 deprivation — which is why deficiency develops slowly and insidiously
b12_biochemistry.absorption_pathway: Food B12 (protein-bound) → GASTRIC ACID and PEPSIN release B12 from food proteins (PPIs and H2 blockers impair this step) → R-PROTEINS (haptocorrins) in saliva initially bind B12 → pancreatic proteases in duodenum degrade R-protein complexes → INTRINSIC FACTOR (IF) from gastric parietal cells binds B12 (loss of parietal cells in autoimmune gastritis = pernicious anaemia) → IF-B12 complex travels to TERMINAL ILEUM → CALCIUM-DEPENDENT receptor (cubilin) on ileal enterocytes absorbs IF-B12 complex (METFORMIN impairs calcium-dependent absorption at this step) → B12 enters portal circulation bound to TRANSCOBALAMIN II (TC-II) → distributed to all cells; PASSIVE ABSORPTION: at very high doses (>1000 mcg), approximately 1% of orally ingested B12 is absorbed passively (without IF) — the basis for high-dose oral B12 therapy

overview.prevalence: Global: approximately 6% of adults under 60 years and 20% over 60 years have biochemical B12 deficiency; India: estimated 47-81% of Indians have B12 insufficiency (<300 pg/mL) and 30-50% have frank deficiency (<200 pg/mL); higher in vegetarian states: Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka; India has the world's highest absolute burden of B12 deficiency — driven by 40% complete vegetarian and 30% lacto-vegetarian population; WHO classifies India as having a severe public health problem of B12 deficiency
overview.age_group: All ages; highest risk: strict vegetarians of all ages; exclusively breastfed infants of B12-deficient vegetarian mothers (severe neonatal B12 deficiency — potentially devastating); elderly (reduced gastric acid impairs absorption); metformin users (all ages); pernicious anaemia predominantly after age 50
overview.is_curable_note: B12 deficiency from dietary causes is fully curable with dietary change and/or supplementation; pernicious anaemia requires lifelong B12 replacement (intrinsic factor permanently absent); neurological damage from prolonged SACD may be only partially reversible — early treatment is essential to prevent permanent neurological disability
overview.key_fact: Vitamin B12 deficiency affects an estimated 47-81% of Indians — making this arguably India's most prevalent and most underdiagnosed nutritional deficiency. It is almost completely PREVENTABLE with daily supplementation costing less than Rs 2-5 per day. The neurological complications — including irreversible spinal cord damage (subacute combined degeneration) and dementia — are the most tragic consequence of delayed diagnosis. Every vegetarian adult in India should take a B12 supplement or consume B12-fortified foods daily.

types.name: Dietary Vitamin B12 Deficiency — Vegetarian and Vegan
types.description: The most common cause of B12 deficiency globally and overwhelmingly the dominant cause in India. Vitamin B12 is naturally present ONLY in animal-derived foods — meat, poultry, fish, seafood, eggs, and dairy products. Plants contain NO biologically available B12. This single fact makes every vegetarian and vegan person at lifelong risk of B12 deficiency. The degree of deficiency risk correlates directly with how completely animal products are excluded from the diet.

risk_stratification_by_diet.b12_intake: Essentially zero from diet; entirely dependent on fortified foods and supplements
risk_stratification_by_diet.deficiency_risk: Extremely high — nearly universal deficiency without supplementation; vegetarians develop deficiency later (years to decades); vegans may develop clinical deficiency faster due to complete animal product elimination
risk_stratification_by_diet.india_prevalence: Growing vegan community in India; very high deficiency rate without supplementation

risk_stratification_by_diet.diet_type: Lacto-Vegetarians (no meat, fish, or eggs — dairy only)
risk_stratification_by_diet.b12_intake: Limited — dairy products contain B12 but: (1) B12 content in Indian dairy (boiled milk, curd, ghee) is reduced by heat treatment and processing; (2) absorption from dairy is less efficient than from meat/fish; (3) quantities consumed often insufficient to meet daily requirements
risk_stratification_by_diet.deficiency_risk: High — the majority of India's vegetarian population; large-scale NNMB (National Nutrition Monitoring Bureau) surveys show 65-70% of lacto-vegetarians in South India are B12 deficient
risk_stratification_by_diet.b12_in_dairy_india: Indian boiled milk contains ~0.4-0.7 mcg B12 per 250 mL glass (daily requirement 2.4 mcg); would need to drink 4-6 glasses of milk daily from B12 alone — practically difficult; curd (yogurt) has slightly less B12 than milk from fermentation; ghee has negligible B12 (fat phase only)

risk_stratification_by_diet.diet_type: Lacto-Ovo-Vegetarians (dairy and eggs — no meat or fish)
risk_stratification_by_diet.b12_intake: Moderate — eggs are a better B12 source than dairy (one large egg provides ~0.6 mcg B12; egg yolk specifically); daily egg consumption combined with dairy may approach requirements
risk_stratification_by_diet.deficiency_risk: Moderate — lower than lacto-vegetarians; but still at risk if consuming eggs infrequently
Low from dietary standpoint alone; risk from other causes (pernicious anaemia, malabsorption, drugs)

types.india_context: India has approximately 400-500 million vegetarians — the world's largest vegetarian population; vegetarianism in India is driven by religious, cultural, and economic factors; many Indians from states like Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra are multigenerational vegetarians; some communities (Jains) practise even stricter dietary restrictions; economic vegetarianism (meat is expensive) creates nutritional vulnerability in low-income populations; dramatic scale of this public health problem has not been adequately addressed in India's national nutrition programmes
types.fermented_foods_myth: Indian fermented foods (idli, dosa, dhokla, kanji, fermented pickles) are sometimes believed to contain significant B12 — this is largely a MYTH; bacterial fermentation can produce B12 analogues (corrinoids) but these are not bioavailable B12 and may even block true B12 absorption; cannot rely on fermented foods for B12

types.name: Pernicious Anaemia (Autoimmune Gastritis — Intrinsic Factor Deficiency)
types.description: Pernicious anaemia (PA) is an autoimmune condition in which T-lymphocyte-mediated destruction of gastric parietal cells and/or antibodies against intrinsic factor (IF) result in complete inability to absorb food-bound B12. 'Pernicious' (meaning fatal) reflects the historical natural history before B12 injection was discovered — an invariably fatal disease now completely manageable with monthly injections. PA accounts for approximately 15-25% of B12 deficiency in non-vegetarian populations in high-income countries; in India its true prevalence is underestimated but increasingly recognised.
types.pathogenesis: Autoimmune gastritis (Type A gastritis) → progressive destruction of corpus/fundal parietal cells → loss of: (1) INTRINSIC FACTOR production (IF is produced exclusively by parietal cells — zero IF = zero B12 absorption); (2) HYDROCHLORIC ACID production (achlorhydria); compensatory G-cell hypergastrinism (elevated serum gastrin); ECL cell hyperplasia → risk of Type 1 gastric carcinoid tumours

antibodies.anti_parietal_cell_antibodies_APCA: Sensitivity 90% for autoimmune gastritis; LOW specificity (false positive in 10-15% of healthy older adults, autoimmune thyroid disease); directed against H+/K+-ATPase (the proton pump) on parietal cells
antibodies.anti_intrinsic_factor_antibodies_AIFA: Type 1 (blocking — prevents B12 binding to IF) and Type 2 (binding — prevents IF-B12 ileal absorption); sensitivity only 50-70% but SPECIFICITY >95% — when positive, virtually diagnostic of pernicious anaemia; the most specific serological test for PA

types.associated_conditions: Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's — 30%; Graves' 10%); Type 1 diabetes; Addison's disease; vitiligo; coeliac disease — all part of autoimmune polyglandular syndromes; family clustering (first-degree relatives 20× higher risk)
types.cancer_risk: Gastric adenocarcinoma (2-3× increased risk from chronic atrophic gastritis); Type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumours (carcinoids from ECL hyperplasia); endoscopic surveillance every 3-5 years recommended
types.treatment: Lifelong IM hydroxocobalamin injections (1000 mcg every 3 months after loading) — since IF is permanently absent, oral B12 from food can never be absorbed; high-dose oral cyanocobalamin (2000 mcg daily) works via passive absorption (1% of oral dose) — an alternative to IM in stable patients without neurological disease

types.name: Drug-Induced B12 Deficiency
types.description: Multiple widely prescribed medications impair B12 absorption through various mechanisms — an important and frequently overlooked cause of B12 deficiency, particularly important in India given the very high prescribing rates of the key culprit drugs.

major_causative_drugs.drug: Metformin — The Most Clinically Important Drug Cause in India
major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Metformin impairs absorption of the IF-B12 complex at the terminal ileum by reducing calcium-dependent endocytosis of cubilin receptors; requires adequate ionised calcium for IF-B12 receptor binding — metformin appears to chelate calcium or reduce its availability at the ileal brush border; the effect is dose-dependent and duration-dependent (cumulative with long-term use)
major_causative_drugs.prevalence: B12 deficiency develops in approximately 10-30% of long-term metformin users (>4 years); higher with higher daily doses; lower B12 (<200 pg/mL) in up to 20% of metformin-treated patients
major_causative_drugs.india_significance: CRITICAL: India has an estimated 80+ million people with Type 2 diabetes; metformin is the first-line medication for T2DM in India and prescribed to almost every newly diagnosed patient; with T2DM itself at epidemic proportions, metformin-induced B12 deficiency represents a massive and growing burden; compounded by high baseline rates of dietary B12 deficiency from vegetarianism
major_causative_drugs.screening_recommendation: Check serum B12 (and ideally MMA) in ALL patients on metformin: at baseline (before starting); at 1 year; then annually; supplement all deficient patients; consider prophylactic supplementation in high-risk groups (vegetarians on metformin)
major_causative_drugs.treatment: Stop metformin if possible (alternative antidiabetics); if metformin must continue — B12 supplementation; oral calcium supplementation (500 mg twice daily with meals) — shown in RCT to partially reverse metformin-induced B12 malabsorption

major_causative_drugs.drug: Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) — Omeprazole, Pantoprazole, Rabeprazole
major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Food-bound B12 requires gastric acid (HCl) and pepsin to cleave it from dietary proteins; PPIs suppress acid production by 90-98% — impairing the initial digestion step that releases food-bound B12 for IF binding; affects food-derived B12 only (crystalline synthetic B12 in supplements is absorbed normally without acid)
major_causative_drugs.prevalence: Clinically significant B12 deficiency from PPI use requires prolonged use (>2 years); develops in approximately 5-10% of long-term PPI users; risk increases with dose and duration
major_causative_drugs.india_significance: PPIs are massively overprescribed in India; very high rates of long-term PPI use without documented indication; compounded by vegetarian diet and frequently concurrent metformin use (triple jeopardy: vegetarian + PPI + metformin)
major_causative_drugs.screening: Annual B12 in any patient on PPIs >2 years, particularly vegetarians

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Same as PPIs but less potent acid suppression — milder B12 malabsorption; less clinically significant than PPIs
major_causative_drugs.note: Ranitidine was withdrawn globally in 2020 due to NDMA contamination

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidises the cobalt atom in methylcobalamin — permanently inactivating the active coenzyme form; even a single prolonged anaesthetic can precipitate acute B12 deficiency-like syndrome (methylcobalamin is required for methionine synthesis for myelin maintenance); acute neurological deterioration post-surgery (particularly orthopaedic spinal surgery) in a B12-deficient patient exposed to N2O can be catastrophic and irreversible
major_causative_drugs.clinical_importance: ALL patients should have B12 checked before elective surgery using nitrous oxide; B12-deficient patients should receive IM B12 before surgery; B12-deficient patients and those with pernicious anaemia should NOT receive nitrous oxide anaesthesia if alternatives available

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Interferes with IF-B12 complex binding to ileal receptors
major_causative_drugs.note: Only with chronic use; monitor B12 annually in long-term colchicine users

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Impairs enterohepatic recycling of B12; binds bile which contains B12 secreted in bile

types.name: Malabsorption Syndromes
types.description: Conditions causing structural or functional impairment of B12 absorption at various steps of the absorption pathway.

causes.details: Total gastrectomy — complete loss of parietal cells → zero IF → zero B12 absorption (same as pernicious anaemia); requires lifelong IM B12; Partial gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y bypass — reduced parietal cell mass → reduced IF → gradual B12 depletion (may take 2-5 years); Bariatric surgery (sleeve gastrectomy, gastric bypass) — significant B12 deficiency in 15-30% without supplementation; ALL bariatric surgery patients need lifelong B12 supplementation

Crohn's disease specifically affecting the terminal ileum — the only site of IF-B12 complex absorption — impairs B12 uptake; ileal resection for Crohn's disease causes permanent B12 malabsorption proportional to the length of ileum resected (>60 cm ileal resection = usually requires IM B12)
Any condition requiring surgical removal or bypass of the terminal ileum; B12 malabsorption is permanent and proportional to extent of ileal loss; requires lifelong IM or high-dose oral B12

Villous atrophy in the small intestine from gluten sensitivity — affects the duodenum and proximal jejunum predominantly; impairs overall nutrient absorption including B12; B12 malabsorption improves with strict gluten-free diet

Overgrowth of bacteria in the small intestine (>100,000 CFU/mL in proximal jejunum) — bacteria consume B12 before it reaches the ileal absorption site; competing for the B12 'share' between bacteria and host; particularly in: diabetic autonomic neuropathy (impaired gut motility); post-surgical blind loops; chronic pancreatitis; scleroderma

A malabsorptive syndrome predominantly affecting people in tropical regions including India — characterised by small intestinal mucosal damage, malabsorption of multiple nutrients including folate and B12, and a megaloblastic anaemia responding to folate and tetracycline; historically important in India; now less commonly diagnosed

Pancreatic proteases in the duodenum are required to release B12 from R-proteins (haptocorrins) so that IF can bind B12 (R-proteins bind B12 more tightly than IF in acidic stomach — proteases in neutral duodenum degrade R-proteins allowing IF to then bind B12); pancreatic insufficiency → R-proteins not degraded → IF cannot compete for B12 → malabsorption

types.name: Functional B12 Deficiency — Normal Serum B12 but Deficient Cellular Function
types.description: A form of B12 deficiency where serum B12 level is in the 'normal' range but intracellular B12 function is impaired — causing all the metabolic and neurological consequences of deficiency despite a reassuringly normal blood test. This is an important and frequently missed diagnosis.
causes: Transcobalamin II (TC-II) deficiency — congenital (rare); TC-II is the transport protein that delivers B12 from gut to cells; without TC-II, B12 cannot enter cells even if serum level appears normal

High holo-TC-I (haptocorrin) — elevated haptocorrin inflates total serum B12 without representing bioavailable B12; common in myeloproliferative disorders, liver disease, and some cancers; can mask true cellular deficiency
Nitrous oxide exposure — inactivates intracellular methylcobalamin while serum total B12 may appear normal; metabolically B12 non-functional
types.diagnosis: Elevated METHYLMALONIC ACID (MMA) and elevated HOMOCYSTEINE despite 'normal' or borderline serum B12 — these functional markers detect cellular deficiency more sensitively than serum B12; HOLOTRANSCOBALAMIN (holo-TC) — the metabolically active fraction of serum B12 bound to TC-II; lower than total B12 and more sensitively reflects available B12

types.name: B12 Deficiency in Pregnancy and Infancy
types.description: Arguably the most critical clinical scenario for B12 deficiency — maternal B12 deficiency during pregnancy has severe consequences for fetal neurological development, and breastfed infants of B12-deficient vegetarian mothers can develop profoundly severe B12 deficiency with devastating neurological consequences within months of birth.

maternal_deficiency.consequences: Neural tube defects (NTDs) — B12 deficiency impairs methionine synthesis → reduces SAM-dependent methylation of folate → functional folate deficiency → impaired neural tube closure; B12 deficiency is an independent risk factor for NTDs even when folate is adequate; elevated homocysteine (from B12 deficiency) is teratogenic; intrauterine growth restriction; increased miscarriage risk; preeclampsia risk; gestational diabetes worsening
maternal_deficiency.india_data: A large study from Pune, India (Yajnik et al.) demonstrated that maternal B12 deficiency is associated with insulin resistance in offspring — the 'thin-fat Indian' phenotype; Indian vegetarian mothers had significantly higher rates of B12 deficiency and higher offspring metabolic disease risk

infant_b12_deficiency.mechanism: Breast milk B12 content directly reflects maternal B12 status; a B12-deficient vegetarian mother produces breast milk with very low B12; exclusively breastfed infants rapidly deplete their already-limited neonatal B12 stores (B12 crosses placenta poorly when maternal levels are deficient)
infant_b12_deficiency.clinical_features: Onset typically 4-12 months of age; initial: irritability, poor feeding, growth failure, hypotonia (floppiness); progression: developmental regression (loss of developmental milestones previously achieved — a devastating sign); seizures; encephalopathy; brain atrophy; if untreated — permanent severe neurological damage; skin hyperpigmentation
infant_b12_deficiency.india_significance: Exclusively breastfed infants of vegetarian Indian mothers are at very high risk; large studies from South India and Maharashtra show significant rates of infantile B12 deficiency with neurological consequences; often diagnosed late (mistaken for genetic neurological disorders); one of India's most preventable causes of developmental disability
infant_b12_deficiency.prevention: All pregnant and breastfeeding vegetarian women in India MUST take B12 supplements (2.6-2.8 mcg or higher as supplement daily OR every-other-day injection); ideally begin before conception; continue throughout breastfeeding

types.supplementation_pregnancy: Folic acid alone is insufficient for vegetarian Indian women — B12 must be combined; the standard ANC (antenatal care) supplement in India (containing iron + folic acid) does NOT contain B12; a significant gap in India's national nutrition programme

severity_levels.name: Subclinical / Biochemical B12 Deficiency
severity_levels.description: Low serum B12 or elevated functional markers (MMA, homocysteine) without clinical symptoms — the most common presentation, detected only on blood testing.
severity_levels.criteria: Serum B12 150-300 pg/mL (borderline-deficient range); OR elevated MMA (>0.4 mcmol/L) and/or homocysteine (>15 mcmol/L) with B12 <300 pg/mL; no haematological abnormalities; no neurological symptoms; often completely asymptomatic
severity_levels.functional_impact: No immediate disability but elevated cardiovascular risk from homocysteinaemia; subclinical cognitive impairment possible; ongoing myelin strain
severity_levels.management: Oral B12 supplementation: cyanocobalamin or methylcobalamin 500-1000 mcg daily; dietary counselling and modification; address underlying cause (medication review); follow-up serum B12 in 3 months to confirm response
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Fatigue, tingling, or cognitive symptoms developing; Hb falling; macrocytosis appearing; B12 falling below 150 pg/mL

severity_levels.name: Mild-Moderate B12 Deficiency — Haematological Manifestations
severity_levels.description: Clinically evident deficiency with megaloblastic anaemia and/or mild neurological symptoms.
severity_levels.criteria: Serum B12 <150-200 pg/mL; macrocytic anaemia (MCV >100 fL); Hb 80-110 g/L; hypersegmented neutrophils on blood film; elevated MMA and homocysteine; mild fatigue, breathlessness, or palpitations; possible mild tingling in extremities; no significant neurological disability
severity_levels.functional_impact: Reduced exercise tolerance; fatigue affecting work; pallor; mild cognitive slowing
severity_levels.management: Oral high-dose B12 (1000-2000 mcg daily) OR IM hydroxocobalamin loading course; investigate and treat underlying cause; folate supplementation if co-existent folate deficiency; monitor reticulocyte response (peak 5-7 days); haemoglobin response over 6-8 weeks

severity_levels.name: Severe B12 Deficiency — Neurological Manifestations (SACD)
severity_levels.description: Advanced deficiency with peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, and/or significant cognitive impairment — the most clinically serious and potentially irreversible presentation.
severity_levels.criteria: Serum B12 usually <100 pg/mL; established peripheral neuropathy (glove-and-stocking sensory loss, areflexia); dorsal column signs (loss of vibration sense and proprioception, Romberg positive, ataxic gait); upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar — late); significant cognitive impairment or psychiatric symptoms; may occur with NORMAL haemoglobin (neurological deficiency can develop without anaemia in 28% of SACD cases)
severity_levels.functional_impact: Significantly impairs ambulation and balance; fall risk; inability to work; cognitive disability; psychiatric symptoms; may be wheelchair-dependent if severe
severity_levels.management: URGENT IM hydroxocobalamin loading (daily injections for 7-14 days); physiotherapy for gait rehabilitation; neurological monitoring; neuropsychological assessment; address cause; neurological recovery: partial over months to years — depends critically on duration of symptoms before treatment; irreversible damage if delayed >12 months
severity_levels.critical_note: Neurological symptoms may WORSEN INITIALLY in the first 1-2 weeks of treatment as remyelination occurs (Uhthoff's phenomenon equivalent); reassure patient and continue treatment

severity_levels.name: Critical — Severe Megaloblastic Crisis or Acute Neurological Deterioration
severity_levels.description: Life-threatening manifestations: severe pancytopaenia with haemodynamic compromise; or acute catastrophic neurological deterioration (such as post-nitrous oxide exposure in undiagnosed deficiency).
severity_levels.criteria: Haemoglobin <60 g/L with cardiovascular compromise; pancytopaenia (Hb <70, WBC <3.0, platelets <50); hypoxia; cardiac arrhythmia from severe anaemia; OR acute paraplegia/tetraplegia post-nitrous oxide exposure in B12-deficient patient; acute psychosis with severe B12 deficiency
severity_levels.management: Emergency hospital admission; blood transfusion if cardiovascular compromise (transfuse slowly — risk of circulatory overload in megaloblastic anaemia with increased plasma volume); IM hydroxocobalamin stat; folate co-supplementation; cardiac monitoring; intensive physiotherapy for neurological deterioration; haematology and neurology involvement

causes.causative_mechanisms: B12 deficiency arises from: (1) INADEQUATE INTAKE — vegetarian/vegan diet; (2) IMPAIRED ABSORPTION — intrinsic factor deficiency (pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy); ileal disease or resection; malabsorption syndromes; medications; (3) INCREASED REQUIREMENTS — pregnancy, lactation; (4) IMPAIRED UTILISATION — transcobalamin II deficiency; (5) INCREASED LOSSES — nitrous oxide inactivation
risk_factors: Strict vegetarian or vegan diet — the single most important risk factor in India; no animal products or minimal animal products = little to no dietary B12; risk increases with strictness of vegetarianism (lacto < lacto-ovo < vegan)

South Asian ethnicity — particularly Indian — from multiple factors: very high vegetarianism rates; cultural food practices; genetic variants in B12 metabolism genes (FUT2, TCN1, MTHFR) prevalent in South Asian populations
Advanced age (>60 years) — progressive gastric atrophy reduces acid and intrinsic factor secretion; impaired appetite; reduced dietary variety; multiple medications
Pregnancy and breastfeeding — increased B12 requirements; depletion of maternal stores for fetal/neonatal needs; exclusively breastfed infants of deficient mothers at extreme risk
Metformin use — see TYPE-03; essential to screen all long-term metformin users; particularly dangerous in vegetarians on metformin (double jeopardy)
Long-term PPI use (>2 years) — impairs food-bound B12 absorption; very common in India; triple jeopardy: vegetarian + PPI + metformin
Pernicious anaemia — autoimmune IF destruction; more common in women; positive family history; associated autoimmune diseases (thyroid, type 1 DM, Addison's, vitiligo)
Gastric surgery — gastrectomy (partial or total); bariatric surgery; all require lifelong B12 supplementation
Terminal ileal disease — Crohn's disease; ileal tuberculosis (in India — an important cause); ileal resection
HIV infection — impaired absorption; dietary deficiency; drug interactions (metformin for HIV-related metabolic syndrome; zidovudine macrocytosis can mask B12-related macrocytosis)
Alcoholism — poor dietary intake; gastric mucosal damage; hepatic B12 store depletion
Tapeworm infestation — Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) competes for B12 in the gut; less common in India but relevant in certain lake-fish-eating communities
Genetic causes — Transcobalamin II deficiency (rare); methylmalonic acidaemia; homocystinuria (severe enzyme defects causing functional B12 deficiency despite normal serum B12)
Poverty and food insecurity — inability to afford animal products; nutritional deficiency complex (B12 + iron + zinc + calcium all affected in poor vegetarians)
Recent immigrants from endemic areas — long-term vegetarians who migrate to Western countries may present with B12 deficiency years later as their reduced stores finally deplete

symptoms.overview: Vitamin B12 deficiency has a remarkably diverse and multisystem clinical presentation — affecting the blood (megaloblastic anaemia), nervous system (peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration, cognitive impairment), and oral mucosa (glossitis). A critically important clinical pearl: neurological manifestations can occur WITHOUT anaemia (in 28% of cases) — the presence of a macrocytic anaemia is neither necessary nor sufficient for the neurological diagnosis; B12 must be checked in any patient with unexplained peripheral neuropathy, cognitive decline, or gait disturbance regardless of haemoglobin level. The onset is insidious — the large hepatic B12 stores mean that deficiency accumulates over 2-5 years before symptoms emerge.

primary_symptoms.name: Fatigue, Weakness, and Exercise Intolerance — Haematological
primary_symptoms.description: The most common presenting complaint — arising from megaloblastic anaemia (defective red blood cell production causing reduced oxygen-carrying capacity). Characteristically described as profound, disproportionate fatigue — far more severe than would be expected from the degree of anaemia on blood count. Pathophysiology: impaired DNA synthesis prevents normal red blood cell maturation → large, fragile, short-lived megaloblastic red cells with reduced functional efficiency → anaemia → tissue hypoxia → fatigue. Associated pallor (pale skin, pale conjunctivae, pale nail beds); breathlessness on exertion; palpitations; dizziness; headache. In severe deficiency: congestive heart failure from high-output cardiac adaptation to chronic severe anaemia.
primary_symptoms.onset: Insidious — develops over months to years as B12 stores are gradually depleted
primary_symptoms.note: 28% of patients with clinically significant B12 deficiency (including SACD) have NO ANAEMIA — neurological symptoms can precede haematological manifestations

primary_symptoms.name: Peripheral Neuropathy — Tingling, Numbness, and Burning in Hands and Feet
primary_symptoms.description: The hallmark early neurological symptom of B12 deficiency — symmetrical sensory disturbance affecting the peripheral nerves, typically beginning in the feet (toes) and ascending proximally ('stocking distribution') before later affecting the hands ('glove distribution') — giving the characteristic 'glove and stocking' pattern of B12 neuropathy. Description: tingling (like electric shocks or pins and needles); numbness (reduced sensation); burning pain (neuropathic pain — particularly in feet at night); cold sensations despite normal temperature. The deficiency affects myelin formation → segmental demyelination of peripheral nerves → impaired sensory conduction. The neuropathy is SENSORY-PREDOMINANT initially — motor weakness appears later in more severe cases. KEY CLINICAL POINT: B12 peripheral neuropathy is frequently misdiagnosed in India as: 'vitamin deficiency neuropathy' (correctly suspected but wrong treatment — often given B1/B6 rather than B12); 'diabetic neuropathy' (particularly common error since B12 deficiency from metformin coexists with DM and produces identical symptoms); 'post-COVID neuropathy'; 'cervical or lumbar spondylitis/myelopathy' (particularly SACD with dorsal column signs).

primary_symptoms.name: Subacute Combined Degeneration of Spinal Cord (SACD) — Dorsal and Lateral Column Demyelination
primary_symptoms.description: The most serious neurological consequence of B12 deficiency — progressive demyelination affecting BOTH the dorsal columns (posterior funiculi — carrying vibration sense and proprioception) AND the lateral columns (corticospinal tracts — carrying motor commands) of the spinal cord. 'Combined' refers to this simultaneous involvement of both columns. DORSAL COLUMN SIGNS (typically first): loss of VIBRATION SENSE (test with 128 Hz tuning fork at great toe, medial malleolus, then tibia; loss of vibration at the toe = earliest sign); loss of PROPRIOCEPTION / joint position sense (ask patient to identify direction of toe movement with eyes closed — cannot detect subtle movements); ROMBERG'S TEST POSITIVE (patient sways significantly or falls when standing with feet together and eyes closed — vision compensates for lost proprioception; closing eyes removes visual compensation); ATAXIC GAIT (wide-based, unsteady gait; difficulty walking in darkness — when vision unavailable for compensation); LATERAL COLUMN SIGNS (later): spastic weakness of legs; hyperreflexia (exaggerated reflexes); EXTENSOR PLANTAR RESPONSE (Babinski sign — abnormal upgoing plantar — indicates corticospinal tract involvement); spastic paraparesis. PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY (concurrent): may reduce deep tendon reflexes (lower motor neuron peripheral neuropathy may MASK the hyperreflexia of lateral column disease — creating the classic combination of reduced reflexes + extensor plantars which is almost pathognomonic of SACD).
primary_symptoms.reversibility: EARLY TREATMENT (within 3-6 months of symptoms): good recovery possible; DELAYED TREATMENT (>6-12 months of symptoms): partial recovery at best; some deficits permanent — particularly proprioceptive loss and ataxia; neurological damage is a RACE AGAINST TIME — B12 must be started urgently on clinical suspicion, before results are available
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: SACD is frequently misdiagnosed in India as: cervical spondylotic myelopathy; hereditary spastic paraplegia; multiple sclerosis; Guillain-Barré syndrome; vitamin E deficiency; copper deficiency (similar dorsal/lateral column pattern); ALWAYS check B12 in any patient with myelopathy of unclear cause

primary_symptoms.name: Cognitive Impairment and Psychiatric Manifestations
primary_symptoms.description: B12 deficiency causes a wide spectrum of neuropsychiatric manifestations — from subtle cognitive slowing through to frank dementia and acute psychosis. COGNITIVE: poor concentration and memory; impaired executive function; slowed mental processing; brain fog (very common — often not attributed to B12 deficiency); over time: progressive dementia (B12 dementia is one of the very few reversible causes of dementia — critically important to detect and treat before irreversibility). PSYCHIATRIC: depression (B12 deficiency impairs serotonin and dopamine synthesis from impaired methylation of neurotransmitter precursors); anxiety; irritability and personality change; acute confusional state; in severe cases: psychiatric psychosis ('megaloblastic madness' — historical term for acute B12-deficiency psychosis, now rare with earlier diagnosis but still seen in severely deprived vegetarian populations or cases of pernicious anaemia). B12-related dementia often presents as: accelerated cognitive decline beyond what is expected for age; cognitive impairment in relatively young individuals (40-60 years); early memory loss and personality change; ALWAYS check B12 in any patient with dementia or cognitive decline — reversible if treated before irreversible neuronal loss occurs.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild (brain fog, depression) to Severe (dementia, psychosis)

primary_symptoms.name: Glossitis — Hunter's or Möller's Glossitis
primary_symptoms.description: A distinctive and diagnostically useful oral mucosal change — the tongue becomes smooth, shiny, and beefy red from atrophy of the normal lingual papillae (the small projections that give the tongue its rough texture). The tongue appears flat and hairless — as though the top surface has been polished — often with a bright red or magenta colour. Painful to eat spicy or acidic foods (the denuded papillae make the tongue very sensitive). Angular cheilitis (redness and cracking at the corners of the mouth) may accompany. These oral changes occur because oral epithelium is among the most rapidly dividing cells in the body — particularly sensitive to DNA synthesis impairment from B12 (or folate) deficiency.
primary_symptoms.note: Glossitis reverses completely within 1-2 weeks of B12 replacement — one of the fastest-responding signs; also seen in iron deficiency, folate deficiency, riboflavin deficiency

secondary_symptoms: Jaundice (mild, lemon-yellow tinge) — from haemolysis within the bone marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis — destruction of abnormal megaloblasts within the marrow before they enter the circulation); elevated bilirubin and LDH; elevated plasma iron from haemolysis

Infertility — both male (impaired spermatogenesis from DNA synthesis failure) and female (impaired folliculogenesis, ovulation, and implantation); B12 deficiency is a treatable and frequently missed cause of unexplained infertility in vegetarian couples

Skin hyperpigmentation — diffuse darkening particularly of knuckles, skin creases, and mucous membranes; melanin overproduction; particularly striking in darker-skinned individuals; may be the presenting sign in infants with B12 deficiency
Weight loss and anorexia — reduced appetite from glossitis and nausea; malabsorption contributing in pernicious anaemia (achlorhydria also reduces protein absorption)
Shortness of breath and palpitations — from anaemia; can be severe in elderly with limited cardiac reserve
Syncope and dizziness — from postural hypotension (autonomic neuropathy) and severe anaemia
Gait disturbance and falls — from ataxia; proprioceptive loss; spastic paraparesis in SACD; major fall risk in elderly B12-deficient patients
Sleep disturbance — from neuropathic pain in feet (worst at night); from mood disturbance (depression, anxiety)
symptoms_in_infants_and_children: Poor feeding, irritability, hypotonia (floppiness) — onset 4-12 months in breastfed infants of deficient vegetarian mothers
Developmental regression — loss of motor, language, and social milestones previously achieved; extremely alarming and requires urgent investigation
Seizures — from metabolic encephalopathy of severe B12 deficiency
Skin hyperpigmentation — characteristic 'dirty skin' appearance over knuckles and skin folds
Poor weight gain and stunted growth

commonly_misdiagnosed_as: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy — SACD dorsal column signs misattributed to neck disease; very common misdiagnosis in India (cervical spondylosis is common; B12 even more common — must always check B12 in myelopathy)
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy — identical sensory symptoms; metformin-taking diabetics at highest risk of B12 neuropathy being missed; check B12 in every diabetic with neuropathy
Post-COVID long haul neuropathy — B12-deficient vegetarians with tingling post-COVID may actually have unmasked pre-existing B12 deficiency
Anxiety and functional neurological disorder — B12 neuropathic tingling is sometimes dismissed as 'anxiety symptoms' particularly in young vegetarian women
Early Parkinson's disease — balance impairment, gait disorder from SACD
Motor neurone disease — mixed UMN and LMN signs in SACD can superficially resemble ALS
Multiple sclerosis — episodic neurological symptoms; young adults; white matter involvement
Age-related cognitive decline / Alzheimer's — B12 dementia mistaken for irreversible dementia

medical_history: Dietary history — THE MOST IMPORTANT QUESTION: 'Are you vegetarian? For how long? Do you eat eggs or dairy? How much dairy per day? Any meat or fish ever?' — this single line of questioning identifies the most common Indian cause; quantify weekly dairy intake
Duration of vegetarianism — longer duration = greater B12 depletion; onset 2-5 years or more after becoming strictly vegetarian
Medication history — metformin (daily dose and duration — critical); PPIs (dose and duration); other drugs (colchicine, cholestyramine, nitrous oxide history for surgery)
Neurological symptoms — tingling, numbness, burning (hands and feet); weakness; balance problems; falls; memory loss; concentration difficulty; depression
Haematological symptoms — fatigue, breathlessness, palpitations, pallor
Oral symptoms — sore tongue; mouth ulcers; angular cheilitis
Family history — pernicious anaemia; autoimmune diseases (thyroid, type 1 DM, Addison's, vitiligo)
Personal autoimmune history — thyroid disease; type 1 DM; Addison's; vitiligo — all associated with pernicious anaemia
GI history — previous gastric surgery; bariatric surgery; Crohn's disease (terminal ileum involvement); coeliac disease; chronic diarrhoea
Pregnancy and obstetric history — previous pregnancies; neural tube defects in offspring (indirect evidence of maternal B12/folate deficiency in previous pregnancy); current pregnancy status
Alcohol history — impairs B12 absorption and hepatic storage
HIV status — increased B12 deficiency risk
Previous B12 testing — if tested before, what was the result? Any treatment given?
Previous anaemia workup — any history of macrocytic anaemia diagnosed
Cognitive history — self-reported or family-reported memory decline; concentration difficulty; personality change; duration
Occupational history — anaesthetic personnel (nitrous oxide exposure)
physical_examination: General appearance — pallor (conjunctival, nail bed, palmar — from anaemia); lemon-yellow tinge (mild jaundice from haemolysis in megaloblastic anaemia); nutritional status; weight loss
Vital signs — tachycardia (compensatory, from anaemia); postural hypotension (autonomic neuropathy from B12 deficiency); heart rate regularity

ORAL EXAMINATION: tongue — inspect for glossitis: smooth, shiny, red, depapillated ('bald tongue' — loss of filiform and fungiform papillae); angular cheilitis (corner-of-mouth cracking and inflammation); oral ulcers

SKIN: pallor; hyperpigmentation (diffuse, particularly knuckles and skin folds — distinctive in darker-skinned patients); jaundice (mild); purpura (thrombocytopaenia from bone marrow failure in severe deficiency)
HAEMATOLOGICAL ASSESSMENT: conjunctival pallor (lower eyelid pulled down — white not pink = anaemia); hepatomegaly (extramedullary haematopoiesis in severe megaloblastic anaemia); splenomegaly (mild)
NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION — THE MOST CRITICAL COMPONENT:

PERIPHERAL NERVOUS SYSTEM: sensory testing — light touch and pinprick in glove-stocking distribution (reduced distally); vibration testing with 128 Hz tuning fork (at great toe → medial malleolus → tibia — reduced or absent at toe in early disease); proprioception (joint position sense — passive movement of great toe with patient eyes closed — cannot detect direction = proprioceptive loss); deep tendon reflexes (diminished or absent in peripheral neuropathy — may mask UMN hyperreflexia)

ROMBERG'S TEST: patient stands with feet together, arms at sides; close eyes; observe for excessive sway or fall = POSITIVE (loss of proprioceptive input with eyes closed; vision was compensating; positive Romberg = dorsal column dysfunction = B12 SACD until proven otherwise)

MOTOR ASSESSMENT: tone (increased = spasticity from lateral column involvement — late sign); power testing (proximal and distal leg weakness from spastic paraparesis); plantar responses (EXTENSOR plantar — Babinski sign — indicates corticospinal tract involvement = SACD confirmed)
GAIT ASSESSMENT: wide-based, unsteady gait; stamping gait (loss of proprioception — patient cannot feel feet properly); tandem gait (walk heel to toe in a straight line — impaired in SACD ataxia)

COGNITIVE ASSESSMENT: informal — orientation, memory (3-word recall, recent events); formal — Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) or Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) for cognitive impairment documentation and monitoring

diagnostic_tests.description: The standard first-line test — but with important limitations. CHEMILUMINESCENT IMMUNOASSAY (CLIA) — the most common laboratory method in India; measures total serum B12 (bound to both transcobalamin II [bioavailable — 20%] and haptocorrin [not bioavailable — 80%]). The normal reference range varies by laboratory but generally: <200 pg/mL = deficiency; 200-300 pg/mL = borderline/indeterminate (many laboratories consider this normal — a significant diagnostic problem); >300 pg/mL = normal. CRITICAL LIMITATIONS: FALSE NORMAL values (serum B12 in 'normal' range despite clinical deficiency): elevated haptocorrin (liver disease, myeloproliferative disorders, some cancers) inflates total B12 without representing bioavailable B12; myeloproliferative disorders classically have very high serum B12 from haptocorrin. FALSE LOW values: folate deficiency can lower serum B12 without true B12 deficiency; pregnancy; oral contraceptive pill. The important clinical rule: if clinical suspicion is HIGH (vegetarian, neuropathy, macrocytosis) and serum B12 is 'normal' but in the 200-350 range — ORDER METHYLMALONIC ACID and HOMOCYSTEINE for functional assessment.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: First-line screening for B12 deficiency; monitoring B12 replacement therapy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: <150 pg/mL = definite deficiency; 150-200 pg/mL = probable deficiency — treat; 200-300 pg/mL = borderline — check MMA and homocysteine; >300 pg/mL = likely adequate (but check functional markers if symptomatic)
diagnostic_tests.india_note: Indian laboratories frequently use different reference ranges; some still use older reference ranges with <180 pg/mL as lower limit of normal — significantly underdiagnosing borderline deficiency; request units in pg/mL or pmol/L explicitly; many Indian labs do not offer MMA — specialist centres only

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Methylmalonic Acid (MMA) — Most Sensitive Functional Marker
diagnostic_tests.description: MMA is the substrate for adenosylcobalamin-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase — when this enzyme is impaired by B12 deficiency, MMA accumulates in blood and urine. Elevated serum MMA is the MOST SENSITIVE and MOST SPECIFIC test for B12 cellular deficiency — detecting functional deficiency before serum B12 becomes overtly low, and confirming deficiency when serum B12 is borderline. A normal MMA (in the absence of renal failure) effectively excludes clinically significant B12 deficiency. An elevated MMA with a 'normal' serum B12 = FUNCTIONAL B12 DEFICIENCY — treat with B12 regardless of serum level.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm B12 deficiency when serum B12 is borderline or when clinical suspicion is high despite normal B12; detect functional deficiency; the gold standard for B12 functional status
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal: <0.28 mcmol/L (some labs: <0.4 mcmol/L); Elevated MMA = B12 functional deficiency (also elevated in renal failure — check creatinine first; elevated MMA with normal renal function = B12 deficiency until proven otherwise)
diagnostic_tests.false_positive: Renal failure — MMA elevated due to reduced excretion (not B12 deficiency); check renal function whenever MMA requested
diagnostic_tests.india_availability: MMA testing available at larger urban reference laboratories (SRL, Thyrocare, Metropolis, Dr Lal PathLabs at select centres); cost approximately Rs 1,500-3,500; increasingly available

diagnostic_tests.description: Homocysteine (an amino acid) is converted to methionine by methylcobalamin-dependent methionine synthase; B12 deficiency impairs this reaction → homocysteine accumulates. Elevated serum homocysteine occurs with: B12 deficiency (most common cause); folate deficiency (cofactor for same reaction); B6 deficiency (secondary pathway); renal failure; hypothyroidism; MTHFR gene polymorphism (C677T — very common in Indians — 10-15% homozygous). Elevated homocysteine is independently associated with increased cardiovascular disease risk (atherosclerosis, thrombosis), increased Alzheimer's disease risk, increased fracture risk, and adverse pregnancy outcomes.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Additional functional marker for B12 (and folate) deficiency; assess cardiovascular risk from hyperhomocysteinaemia; monitor response to B12 replacement (homocysteine normalises within 2-4 weeks of effective treatment)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal: <15 mcmol/L (some guidelines <12 mcmol/L for optimal); Mildly elevated: 15-30; Moderately elevated: 30-100; Severely elevated: >100 (uncommon — suggests homocystinuria, severe deficiency, or renal failure)
diagnostic_tests.not_specific_for_b12: Elevated homocysteine from folate or B6 deficiency — give both B12 AND folate empirically when elevated (folate deficiency often coexists)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Full Blood Count (FBC), Blood Film, and MCV
diagnostic_tests.description: The classic haematological signature of B12 (or folate) deficiency is MEGALOBLASTIC ANAEMIA — characterised by specific blood count and morphological changes. BLOOD COUNT: elevated MCV (mean corpuscular volume >100 fL — MACROCYTOSIS: large red cells; normal MCV 80-100 fL); decreased Hb (anaemia — may be severe); WBC may be low (leukopenia); platelets may be low (thrombocytopaenia) — PANCYTOPAENIA in severe deficiency from global bone marrow failure. BLOOD FILM (peripheral smear) — THE MOST DIAGNOSTICALLY USEFUL TEST: OVAL MACROCYTES (large, oval-shaped red cells — macro-ovalocytes — distinct from round macrocytes of liver disease or alcohol); HYPERSEGMENTED NEUTROPHILS — the most specific haematological finding of megaloblastic anaemia: neutrophil nuclei with ≥5 lobes (normal maximum 4 lobes; >4% of neutrophils with 5 lobes, or any neutrophil with 6+ lobes = DIAGNOSTIC of megaloblastic anaemia); DIMORPHIC PICTURE (mixed macrocytes and microcytes when coexistent iron deficiency — 'double deficiency' very common in Indian vegetarians — combined B12/folate + iron deficiency; may paradoxically have NORMAL MCV despite megaloblastic bone marrow as the two effects cancel out).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect megaloblastic anaemia; identify macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils; quantify severity of anaemia; detect pancytopaenia; identify concurrent iron deficiency
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: MCV >100 fL = macrocytosis; >110 fL = suggests megaloblastic rather than simple macrocytosis; Hypersegmented neutrophils (>4% with ≥5 lobes) = megaloblastic = B12 or folate deficiency
diagnostic_tests.critical_caveat: 28% of patients with confirmed B12 deficiency including SACD have NORMAL haemoglobin and NORMAL MCV — DO NOT rely on anaemia or macrocytosis to rule out B12 deficiency; check B12 in ALL patients with neurological symptoms suspicious of deficiency

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Folate and Red Cell Folate
diagnostic_tests.description: Folate and B12 deficiency both cause identical megaloblastic anaemia — they must be distinguished because the management differs critically. CRITICAL WARNING: giving FOLATE ALONE to a patient with B12 deficiency can correct the haematological (blood count) abnormalities but allows or even ACCELERATES the neurological deterioration from B12 deficiency — 'masking' the megaloblastic anaemia while the spinal cord continues to demyelinate. Always give BOTH B12 AND FOLATE when megaloblastic anaemia is identified and before results are available (safer than waiting). Serum folate reflects recent dietary folate intake (last few days); red cell folate reflects longer-term folate status.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Distinguish B12 from folate deficiency; identify combined deficiency (common in Indian vegetarians who have low intake of both); avoid the dangerous error of treating B12 deficiency with folate alone
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Serum folate <3 mcg/L = deficiency; Red cell folate <150 mcg/L = deficiency; give both B12 and folate empirically when megaloblastic anaemia diagnosed

diagnostic_tests.description: Iron deficiency frequently coexists with B12 (and folate) deficiency in Indian vegetarians — as all three nutrients are predominantly from animal-derived foods. The 'double deficiency' of B12 + iron creates a DIMORPHIC BLOOD PICTURE (mixture of large megaloblastic cells and small microcytic iron-deficient cells) — the MCV may be paradoxically normal or even low despite significant megaloblastic bone marrow pathology. ALWAYS check iron studies (ferritin, serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation) in all patients with suspected or confirmed B12 deficiency — particularly vegetarians.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect concurrent iron deficiency; explain dimorphic blood picture; guide comprehensive nutritional replacement
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Ferritin <15 mcg/L = iron deficiency; Ferritin <30 mcg/L with symptoms = functional iron deficiency

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Anti-Parietal Cell Antibodies (APCA) and Anti-Intrinsic Factor Antibodies (AIFA)
diagnostic_tests.description: Serological tests for autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia). APCA: sensitivity 90% for autoimmune gastritis; low specificity (false positive in 10-15% of healthy older women, autoimmune thyroid disease); not alone diagnostic of pernicious anaemia. AIFA TYPE 1 (blocking antibody): sensitivity 50-70%; SPECIFICITY >95% — when positive, virtually diagnostic of pernicious anaemia; the most clinically useful single test for PA. Negative AIFA does NOT exclude PA (50% of PA patients are antibody-negative on testing).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose pernicious anaemia (autoimmune intrinsic factor deficiency); guide long-term treatment decisions (lifelong IM B12 vs oral supplementation); identify associated autoimmune disease risk
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: AIFA positive (either type) = pernicious anaemia diagnosis confirmed with >95% certainty; APCA positive alone = screen further (low specificity)
diagnostic_tests.when_to_test: Non-vegetarians with B12 deficiency (dietary cause unlikely — pernicious anaemia or malabsorption more likely); patients with associated autoimmune diseases; older adults with B12 deficiency and atrophic gastritis features; unexplained or severe B12 deficiency

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Gastrin and Pepsinogen I / Pepsinogen I:II Ratio
diagnostic_tests.description: Markedly elevated serum gastrin (>200 pg/mL; often >500-2000 pg/mL) in the setting of B12 deficiency indicates autoimmune gastritis with achlorhydria — supporting pernicious anaemia diagnosis (acid inhibition removes negative feedback on antral G-cells → hypergastrinaemia). Low pepsinogen I (<70 mcg/L) and low PGI/PGII ratio (<3) indicate corpus atrophy (loss of chief cells and parietal cells in the gastric body).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Support diagnosis of autoimmune gastritis/pernicious anaemia; assess severity of gastric atrophy; non-invasive gastric cancer risk stratification
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Gastrin >200 pg/mL + B12 deficiency (in non-PPI user) = autoimmune gastritis likely

diagnostic_tests.description: Bone marrow examination in B12 deficiency shows the classic MEGALOBLASTIC changes: giant metamyelocytes (precursor neutrophils with horseshoe-shaped nuclei — pathognomonic); megaloblasts (abnormally large erythroid precursors with fine open nuclear chromatin — 'salt and pepper' pattern — despite advanced cytoplasmic haemoglobin); hypercellular marrow (erythroid hyperplasia — 'pernicious anaemia picture'). Bone marrow biopsy is now RARELY required for diagnosing B12 deficiency — serum B12, MMA, blood film, and a therapeutic trial with rapid haematological response have replaced marrow examination in most cases. Perform bone marrow examination when: the diagnosis remains uncertain despite blood tests; concurrent haematological malignancy suspected; unusual blood film findings.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm megaloblastic anaemia when diagnosis uncertain; exclude haematological malignancy

diagnostic_tests.description: Holotranscobalamin (holo-TC or Active-B12) measures only the B12 fraction bound to transcobalamin II — the metabolically active and deliverable fraction (representing only 20% of total serum B12). This is the fraction that is taken up by all body cells. Holo-TC is the EARLIEST marker of developing B12 deficiency — it falls before serum total B12, MMA, or homocysteine become abnormal. Normal: >35 pmol/L; deficient: <20 pmol/L; borderline: 20-35 pmol/L.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Earliest sensitive indicator of depleting B12 stores; detect B12 depletion before overt deficiency; preferred in high-risk populations for early screening (vegetarians, elderly, metformin users)
diagnostic_tests.india_availability: Limited availability in India — available at some reference laboratories; gradually becoming more accessible

diagnostic_tests.test_name: MRI Brain and Spinal Cord — Neurological B12 Deficiency
diagnostic_tests.description: MRI of the brain and spinal cord is indicated in patients with established or suspected SACD or significant cognitive impairment from B12 deficiency. SPINAL CORD MRI (T2-weighted): shows characteristic HIGH SIGNAL in the dorsal columns (posterior funiculi) of the spinal cord — most pronounced in the cervical and thoracic spine; the 'inverted V sign' (bilateral symmetrical T2 hyperintensity in the posterior cord) is strongly suggestive of SACD; changes may also appear in the lateral columns in more advanced disease. BRAIN MRI: white matter T2 hyperintensities (subcortical and periventricular leukoencephalopathy); cortical atrophy (in dementia from B12 deficiency); these brain changes may partially reverse with B12 treatment. MRI is also important to EXCLUDE other causes of myelopathy (MS, tumour, arteriovenous malformation, cervical cord compression) in the differential diagnosis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm SACD; characterise extent of neurological involvement; exclude alternative causes of myelopathy; baseline for monitoring treatment response
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: T2 hyperintensity in dorsal (posterior) columns of cervical and thoracic spinal cord = SACD characteristic finding
diagnostic_tests.india_note: Spinal cord MRI is the investigation that can clinch the SACD diagnosis in a B12-deficient patient with neurological signs — particularly useful when differentiating from cervical spondylotic myelopathy (spondylosis shows cord compression/signal at disc level; SACD shows diffuse posterior column signal without focal compression)

diagnostic_tests.description: Electrophysiological assessment of peripheral nerve function — useful to confirm and characterise B12 peripheral neuropathy. NCS in B12 neuropathy: reduced sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) amplitudes (axonal loss component); reduced or absent sensory nerve conduction velocities; later — motor nerve involvement; pattern: predominantly sensory, symmetrical, distal; similar to but distinct from diabetic neuropathy (pure demyelinating pattern less common in B12 than in CIDP). May be entirely NORMAL in early B12 deficiency (the sensory symptoms may precede electrophysiological changes).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Characterise and confirm peripheral neuropathy; document severity for baseline and follow-up comparison; distinguish B12 neuropathy from other causes (diabetic, CIDP, toxic, hereditary)

medicines.note: Treatment of B12 deficiency is straightforward and highly effective when initiated promptly — the key decisions are: (1) ROUTE: IM injection vs high-dose oral vs sublingual — all effective; IM is essential for pernicious anaemia and severe neurological disease; high-dose oral works for most dietary deficiency; (2) FORM: hydroxocobalamin (preferred IM) vs cyanocobalamin (most commonly used oral) vs methylcobalamin (active form — widely used in India); (3) DURATION: lifelong for pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy, and other permanent malabsorption causes; until repletion and dietary correction for simple dietary deficiency; (4) CONCURRENT TREATMENT: always give folate (5 mg/day) when treating megaloblastic anaemia — the reverse is dangerous (folate alone in B12 deficiency). The haematological response is gratifyingly rapid — reticulocyte peak at 5-7 days; haemoglobin normalises over 6-8 weeks. Neurological response is slower and depends entirely on how long deficiency was present before treatment.

treatment_response_timeline.day_3_to_5: Subjective improvement in energy and well-being
treatment_response_timeline.day_5_to_7: RETICULOCYTE PEAK — the bone marrow responds and pours out new red cells (reticulocyte count rises to 20-40%; normal <2%); this confirms the diagnosis retrospectively and confirms adequate treatment
treatment_response_timeline.week_2: Glossitis healing; serum iron may fall as iron is used for haemoglobin synthesis (relative iron deficiency — may need iron supplementation)
treatment_response_timeline.week_4_to_8: Haemoglobin normalisation (if iron stores adequate); white cells and platelets normalise within 2 weeks
treatment_response_timeline.months_3_to_6: Neurological improvement begins — tingling and numbness improve first; proprioception and balance improve more slowly
treatment_response_timeline.months_6_to_18: Maximum neurological recovery achieved — deficits present for more than 6-12 months before treatment may be permanent

categories.category_name: Intramuscular (IM) Vitamin B12 — Hydroxocobalamin (First-Line for Neurological Disease and Pernicious Anaemia)
categories.purpose: Bypasses all oral absorption steps — delivers B12 directly into circulation regardless of intrinsic factor or intestinal function; essential for: pernicious anaemia (no IF — oral absorption impossible); severe neurological disease (SACD); post-gastrectomy; terminal ileal disease; any situation where rapid, reliable repletion is needed.

medicines.name: Hydroxocobalamin Injection
brand_examples: Hydroxocobalamin injection 1000 mcg/mL — NHS standard; available in India at major hospital pharmacies; some brand names: Cyanokit (high dose for cyanide poisoning — different indication); Hydroxocobalamin ampoules
medicines.form: IM injection (1 mL ampoule containing 1000 mcg hydroxocobalamin)

dosage.loading_for_deficiency_with_neurological: 1000 mcg IM daily × 14 days (intensive loading to rapidly replenish stores and provide substrate for urgent remyelination)
dosage.loading_for_deficiency_without_neurologi: 1000 mcg IM every other day × 6 doses (UK guidelines) OR 1000 mcg IM daily × 7 days
dosage.maintenance_pernicious_anaemia_or_perman: 1000 mcg IM every 3 months LIFELONG (hydroxocobalamin tissue retention is excellent — 3-monthly injections maintain adequate stores)
dosage.maintenance_dietary_deficiency_after_loa: 1000 mcg IM every 3 months until dietary B12 is reliably adequate; then switch to oral supplementation

medicines.mechanism: Hydroxocobalamin has the highest tissue binding and retention of all injectable B12 forms; 1000 mcg dose provides serum levels far exceeding normal to saturate body stores; intracellular conversion to active forms (methylcobalamin, adenosylcobalamin) occurs naturally
medicines.advantage_over_cyanocobalamin_im: Longer tissue retention — hydroxocobalamin stays in the body 3× longer than cyanocobalamin; thus 3-monthly hydroxocobalamin vs monthly cyanocobalamin injections are equivalent; hydroxocobalamin is PREFERRED for pernicious anaemia maintenance in UK and most European guidelines; hydroxocobalamin also binds and removes cyanide (relevant in smoke inhalation — dual function)
medicines.injection_technique: IM injection into the deltoid (upper arm) or gluteus (buttock); rotate sites; 1 mL volume tolerated well IM; warn patient of temporary red urine (excess B12 excreted renally — harmless) and possible injection site soreness
medicines.india_availability: Hydroxocobalamin injection is less commonly stocked in India than cyanocobalamin; many Indian hospitals use cyanocobalamin injections; seek hydroxocobalamin at specialist pharmacies or hospital dispensaries; increasingly available

medicines.name: Cyanocobalamin Injection — Alternative IM Form
brand_examples: Cyanocobalamin injection 1000 mcg/mL — widely available India
Neurobion injection (contains B1, B6, and cyanocobalamin — combination)
medicines.dosage: Loading: 1000 mcg IM daily × 7 days; Maintenance (pernicious anaemia): 1000 mcg IM MONTHLY (shorter retention than hydroxocobalamin — requires monthly not quarterly injections)
medicines.india_note: Cyanocobalamin injection is the most readily available injectable B12 form in India; equally effective for repletion but requires more frequent maintenance dosing (monthly vs quarterly for hydroxocobalamin); Neurobion (B1+B6+B12 combination) is very widely used in India but contains only 1000 mcg B12 per injection — appropriate for B12 deficiency; the B1 and B6 components are not needed for isolated B12 deficiency but harmless

categories.purpose: High-dose oral B12 exploits PASSIVE ABSORPTION — approximately 1% of any orally administered B12 is absorbed by passive diffusion without requiring intrinsic factor; at high doses (1000-2000 mcg), this 1% represents 10-20 mcg — well above daily requirements. This approach is effective even in pernicious anaemia (IF absent) and ileal disease, provided the dose is high enough. Multiple RCTs have shown high-dose oral B12 (2000 mcg/day) equivalent to IM B12 in achieving haematological and neurological recovery for mild-moderate non-emergency deficiency.

medicines.name: Cyanocobalamin Oral Tablets — High-Dose
brand_examples: Cyanocobalamin 500 mcg, 1000 mcg tablets — various Indian brands

dosage.treatment_of_deficiency: 1000-2000 mcg ONCE DAILY (not twice daily — once daily is adequate due to saturation of ileal receptors and passive absorption kinetics); continue for minimum 3-6 months for repletion
dosage.prevention_supplementation: 500-1000 mcg once daily for vegetarians and high-risk groups
dosage.elderly: 1000 mcg once daily (impaired gastric acid reduces food-bound B12 absorption but crystalline supplement B12 is less acid-dependent)

medicines.effectiveness_caveat: High-dose oral B12 is appropriate for: dietary deficiency where compliance with injections is a concern; stable pernicious anaemia without active neurological disease; maintenance after IM loading; patients refusing injections. MUST USE INJECTIONS FOR: active SACD/significant neurological disease (need rapid reliable high tissue delivery); severe megaloblastic crisis; doubt about compliance with oral medication
medicines.india_note: Oral cyanocobalamin 500 mcg tablets widely available at all chemists in India; cost approximately Rs 2-5 per tablet (500 mcg) — extremely affordable; a major barrier is simply awareness that B12 supplementation is needed

medicines.name: Methylcobalamin Oral Tablets / Sublingual
brand_examples: Mecobalamin 500 mcg, 1500 mcg — very widely prescribed in India
medicines.form: Tablet (500 mcg, 1500 mcg); Sublingual tablet (dissolves under tongue without swallowing)
medicines.dosage: 500 mcg once or twice daily (for maintenance); 1500 mcg once daily (treatment dose); sublingual: 1000 mcg once daily
medicines.mechanism: Methylcobalamin is the ACTIVE COENZYME FORM of B12 — does not require hepatic conversion before cellular use; widely used in India and Japan for B12 deficiency and neuropathy; some evidence that methylcobalamin may be superior to cyanocobalamin for NERVE REPAIR (promotes axonal regeneration in peripheral nerves); sublingual administration bypasses gastric absorption and may have higher bioavailability in conditions of impaired gastric function
medicines.india_note: Methylcobalamin is THE most widely prescribed B12 supplement in India — prescribed by neurologists, GPs, diabetologists, and orthopaedic surgeons for neuropathic symptoms; very widely available; preferred by many Indian clinicians for neurological B12 deficiency
medicines.comparison: Both cyanocobalamin and methylcobalamin are effective for treating B12 deficiency; cyanocobalamin is cheaper and more stable (preferred by WHO and UK guidelines); methylcobalamin is preferred by many Asian and Indian clinicians for neuropathy; both are acceptable at equivalent doses
medicines.sublingual_advantage: Sublingual B12 is absorbed directly through oral mucosa — bypassing gastric acid, intrinsic factor, and ileal receptors entirely; useful in patients with malabsorption or pernicious anaemia who prefer not to inject; comparable to IM in some studies

categories.category_name: Folic Acid — Always Co-Prescribe with B12 in Megaloblastic Anaemia
categories.purpose: Co-prescription with B12 in megaloblastic anaemia — to: (1) treat concurrent folate deficiency (very common in Indian vegetarians); (2) provide the functional folate cycle substrate that is restored by B12 treatment; (3) prevent the 'masking' danger of isolated folate administration. CRITICAL WARNING: NEVER give FOLATE ALONE when B12 deficiency is suspected — the anaemia will improve but the neurological deterioration will continue or worsen unchecked.

medicines.name: Folic Acid
medicines.dosage: Treatment of folate deficiency or megaloblastic anaemia: 5 mg once daily × 4 months; Prevention/supplementation: 400 mcg once daily (general adults); 400-800 mcg daily (women planning pregnancy — ideally 3 months pre-conception and throughout first trimester); 5 mg daily during pregnancy for high-risk (prior NTD, methotrexate use, malabsorption)
medicines.concurrent_b12: Always prescribe B12 TOGETHER with folate when treating megaloblastic anaemia; give B12 AND folate from the outset — then adjust based on which was the primary deficiency

categories.purpose: Treat the very common concurrent iron deficiency in vegetarian patients with B12 deficiency — as B12 treatment corrects megaloblastic anaemia and the bone marrow resumes normal erythropoiesis, massive iron utilisation may deplete available iron ('iron hunger' of recovering marrow) causing secondary iron-deficiency anaemia during treatment.

medicines.name: Ferrous Sulphate / Ferrous Fumarate / Ferric Glycine Sulphate
medicines.dosage: Ferrous sulphate 200 mg (65 mg elemental iron) twice daily with food and Vitamin C; continue for 3-6 months until ferritin normalised
medicines.use_case: All vegetarian B12-deficient patients with concurrent iron deficiency (ferritin <30 mcg/L); patients developing 'iron hunger' during B12 treatment (falling reticulocyte response despite adequate B12 = iron limiting recovery)

categories.category_name: Prevention — B12 Supplements for At-Risk Groups
categories.purpose: Prophylactic B12 supplementation for all vegetarians, vegans, and high-risk individuals — one of the most cost-effective public health interventions available in India.

medicines.name: Cyanocobalamin 500-1000 mcg Daily — For All Vegetarians in India
medicines.dosage: Vegetarians and vegans: 500-1000 mcg orally once daily (far exceeds daily requirement — ensures sufficient passive absorption); Pregnant vegetarians: at least 1000 mcg daily (ideally start before conception); Lactating vegetarians: 1000 mcg daily (to maintain adequate breast milk B12 for infant); Elderly vegetarians: 1000 mcg daily (impaired gastric acid + reduced intake); Metformin users: 1000 mcg daily if on metformin >2 years regardless of vegetarianism; Long-term PPI users: 1000 mcg daily if on PPIs >2 years
medicines.india_public_health_recommendation: India needs a national B12 supplementation and food fortification programme; current ANC supplements (IFA tablets) do NOT contain B12 — a critical gap in maternal nutrition support; many experts recommend mandatory B12 fortification of common foods in India (salt, flour, milk)
medicines.cost_effectiveness: Cost of B12 deficiency in India: neurological disability, anaemia-related lost productivity, developmental disability in infants, increased cardiovascular disease from homocysteinaemia; cost of daily supplementation: Rs 1.5-3 per day (500 mcg cyanocobalamin tablet) = approximately Rs 700-1100/year; one of the most cost-effective preventive health interventions available

medicines.name: B12-Fortified Foods — Emerging Prevention Strategy
medicines.description: Foods commercially fortified with B12 — an alternative to supplementation tablets that requires no individual compliance. Examples: fortified breakfast cereals (Kellogg's and similar — fortified at 25-100% DV per serving); fortified plant milks (soy milk, oat milk, almond milk — fortified at 50-100% DV per serving); nutritional yeast (fortified with B12 — popular among vegans globally; use in Indian cooking as flavour enhancer); fortified flour (theoretical — not yet widely implemented in India); B12-fortified salt (proposed as low-cost delivery vehicle).
medicines.india_availability: B12-fortified foods are available but expensive and not widely accessible in rural India or low-income populations; fortified cereals in urban supermarkets; policy advocacy needed for affordable B12 fortification of widely consumed staple foods

medicines.name: Calcium Supplementation (500 mg Twice Daily with Meals) — For Metformin-Induced B12 Malabsorption
medicines.dosage: 500 mg elemental calcium twice daily with meals
medicines.evidence: RCT by Bauman et al. showed that calcium supplementation partially reversed metformin-induced B12 malabsorption — by providing the calcium ions required for calcium-dependent IF-B12 receptor (cubilin) function at the terminal ileum; useful adjunct when metformin cannot be reduced
medicines.note: Does not replace B12 supplementation in deficient patients — use as an adjunct; helps prevent ongoing malabsorption while maintaining metformin therapy

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet is both the cause and the solution for the majority of B12 deficiency in India. Since B12 is present ONLY in animal products, dietary management means either: (1) incorporating animal-source foods into the diet (where culturally, religiously, and personally acceptable); or (2) consuming B12-fortified foods; or (3) supplementing with B12 tablets — which is the most practical, reliable, and affordable approach for most Indian vegetarians. Nutritional counselling should emphasise that B12 is the ONLY nutrient that cannot be reliably obtained from a purely plant-based diet — other nutrients (iron, zinc, calcium, omega-3, protein) can be obtained from diverse plant sources, but B12 cannot.

highest_sources.notes: Not part of typical Indian diet but clams (tepi/khube in coastal India — Maharashtra, Goa, Kerala) are exceptional B12 source
Highest B12 among commonly consumed foods; 30g chicken liver = 3 days B12 requirement; organ meats consumed in many non-vegetarian Indian communities
Excellent B12 source; widely available in coastal India; affordable; bangda (Indian mackerel), rohu, hilsa — all good sources
The most accessible animal-source B12 for many Indian lacto-ovo-vegetarians; egg yolk contains virtually all the B12; one egg per day provides ~25% daily requirement
Would need 2+ glasses daily for adequate B12 from milk alone; boiling reduces B12 by 20-30% (traditional Indian practice of boiling milk before drinking)
Better B12 source per gram than milk; popular Indian food; 100g paneer daily provides ~25% B12 requirement
Similar to milk; daily curd consumption is a good practice but alone insufficient for total B12 needs
Good B12 source but high in saturated fat and sodium; limited daily consumption appropriate

negligible_or_zero_sources: All plant foods: vegetables, fruits, grains, legumes, nuts, seeds — ZERO bioavailable B12
Fermented plant foods: idli, dosa, dhokla, pickles, tofu — contain B12 analogues (corrinoids) not bioavailable B12 — CANNOT meet requirements
Plant milks (soy, almond, oat, coconut) unless FORTIFIED — ZERO B12
